sections.title: Riverbank Community Sports Centre
sections.context: Daniel vừa chuyển đến khu Riverbank và gọi điện tới trung tâm thể thao cộng đồng để hỏi thủ tục đăng ký thẻ hội viên.

transcript.speaker: Kirsty
transcript.text: Good morning, Riverbank Community Sports Centre, Kirsty speaking. How can I help you?

transcript.speaker: Daniel
transcript.text: Oh, hello. I've just moved to Riverbank and a neighbour said I should ring about joining the centre.

transcript.speaker: Kirsty
transcript.text: Of course. I can take your details over the phone now and start a provisional record, and then you simply finish it off when you come in for the first time.

transcript.speaker: Daniel
transcript.text: That sounds easy enough. Go ahead.

transcript.speaker: Kirsty
transcript.text: Right. Could I take your full name first?

transcript.speaker: Daniel
transcript.text: Yes, it's Daniel Whitfield.

transcript.speaker: Kirsty
transcript.text: Daniel, lovely. And how do you spell the surname? Is that W-H-I-T-E?

transcript.speaker: Daniel
transcript.text: No, there's no E in the middle. It's W-H-I-T-F-I-E-L-D. Whitfield.

transcript.speaker: Kirsty
transcript.text: Whitfield, thank you. And what's your address here in Riverbank?

transcript.speaker: Daniel
transcript.text: Well, I was at 12 Marlow Street until last month, but the new place is 42 Harlow Road.

transcript.speaker: Kirsty
transcript.text: Sorry, did you say Marlow Road?

transcript.speaker: Daniel
transcript.text: No, Harlow. H-A-R-L-O-W. Harlow Road, and the number is 42.

transcript.speaker: Kirsty
transcript.text: Got it, 42 Harlow Road. And the best number to reach you on during the day?

transcript.speaker: Daniel
transcript.text: The landline isn't connected yet, so you'd better take my mobile. It's 07862 445109 — oh, hang on, I always turn those last digits round. It's 07862 445190.

transcript.speaker: Kirsty
transcript.text: 07862 445190. That's on the record. Now, would you like me to run through the three levels of membership?

transcript.speaker: Daniel
transcript.text: Yes, please, because the website confused me slightly.

transcript.speaker: Kirsty
transcript.text: It confuses everybody. Bronze is weekends only, and that's twenty-two pounds a month. Silver gives you the gym, the pool and the running track on weekday afternoons before four o'clock, as well as the whole weekend. Gold is unlimited access at any hour, plus all the fitness classes.

transcript.speaker: Daniel
transcript.text: Hmm. Gold sounds tempting, but I start work at half past eight and I'm rarely home before six, so I'd never use the daytime... Actually, no, hold on. I work from home on Mondays and Fridays, so weekday afternoons would suit me perfectly. Let's say Silver.

transcript.speaker: Kirsty
transcript.text: Silver it is. That works out at £36.50 a month by direct debit. It was £34.50 last year, but all our prices went up in April, I'm afraid.

transcript.speaker: Daniel
transcript.text: £36.50 is still cheaper than the gym I left behind.

transcript.speaker: Kirsty
transcript.text: And when would you like the membership to begin? I can start you from 30 September, but then you'd pay for a part month, so most people prefer to wait for the billing run.

transcript.speaker: Daniel
transcript.text: When is the next one?

transcript.speaker: Kirsty
transcript.text: The next one goes through on 14 October.

transcript.speaker: Daniel
transcript.text: Then let's make it 14 October. There's no rush.

transcript.speaker: Kirsty
transcript.text: Lovely. Now, two things to note before your first session. Every new member is entitled to a free induction. It used to be run by a volunteer, but these days one of our instructors takes you round the gym and writes a programme for you. It lasts about forty minutes.

transcript.speaker: Daniel
transcript.text: Do I have to book that in advance?

transcript.speaker: Kirsty
transcript.text: No, you can arrange it on the day. The other thing is the lockers. We do sell padlocks at reception for two pounds, but they run out constantly, so if you can, bring a padlock of your own.

transcript.speaker: Daniel
transcript.text: A padlock. I'm writing that down.

transcript.speaker: Kirsty
transcript.text: May I ask what made you decide to join? It's for our funding report, so you can say anything you like.

transcript.speaker: Daniel
transcript.text: Well, several people have told me a sports centre is a good way to meet people in a new town, and of course I'd like to be fitter in general. But the honest answer is my knee. I had an operation on it in June and the physiotherapist wants me in the pool three times a week.

transcript.speaker: Kirsty
transcript.text: Then the early swim will suit you. The pool is quietest between seven and eight in the morning, before the school groups arrive.

transcript.speaker: Daniel
transcript.text: Good to know. Is there anything I need to do before I turn up?

transcript.speaker: Kirsty
transcript.text: You can download our app, and the class timetable lives on the website. You don't need proof of address, by the way — the postcode is enough for us. But the one essential thing is to call in at reception, because we have to take your photograph for the membership card.

transcript.speaker: Daniel
transcript.text: Can't I send one in by email?

transcript.speaker: Kirsty
transcript.text: I'm afraid not. The barriers read the photo card, so nobody gets through the gate without one, and people are caught out by that every single week.

transcript.speaker: Daniel
transcript.text: So, photograph first, everything else afterwards.

transcript.speaker: Kirsty
transcript.text: Exactly. Reception is open from seven in the morning until nine at night, seven days a week.

transcript.speaker: Daniel
transcript.text: Brilliant. Thank you for your help, Kirsty.

transcript.speaker: Kirsty
transcript.text: You're very welcome, Daniel. We'll see you on the fourteenth.

sections.title: Hollow Hill Botanic Garden
sections.context: Một hướng dẫn viên giới thiệu với nhóm khách tham quan về lịch sử, các khu vườn và thông tin thực tế của vườn thực vật Hollow Hill.

transcript.speaker: Alison
transcript.text: Good morning everybody, and welcome to Hollow Hill Botanic Garden. My name is Alison and I train the volunteer guides here, so I'll give you a short introduction and then set you free to explore on your own.

transcript.speaker: Alison
transcript.text: Almost every visitor says the same thing at the gate: that the garden looks as though it has been growing here for centuries.

transcript.speaker: Alison
transcript.text: In fact, until 1890 the entire site was a working limestone quarry, and that pale cliff behind the café is not a natural feature at all. It is the old quarry face, cut by hand.

transcript.speaker: Alison
transcript.text: The Hollow family, who farmed the land above us, bought the pit in 1891 and planted trees in it as a private hobby. It passed to the city council, and to the public, in 1954.

transcript.speaker: Alison
transcript.text: You will all have come in through our new visitor centre. We're extremely proud of it, although I have to admit it caused us a good deal of trouble.

transcript.speaker: Alison
transcript.text: Most of the money came from a lottery grant, about a fifth was raised by donations, and the roof timber came from our own storm-damaged beech trees.

transcript.speaker: Alison
transcript.text: We had hoped to welcome you into it last spring, but the wettest winter anyone remembers flooded the foundations twice, and the doors did not open until September.

transcript.speaker: Alison
transcript.text: A word now for those of you who have brought young children with you today.

transcript.speaker: Alison
transcript.text: The lake path looks tempting, I know, but it is narrow, it has no fence on the water side and the boards are slippery for small feet.

transcript.speaker: Alison
transcript.text: I'd send you instead to the play trail in the north field, which has climbing logs and a gate at each end. The two o'clock tour lasts ninety minutes and is really designed for adults.

transcript.speaker: Alison
transcript.text: Now, if you only have time for one building, make it the Glasshouse, which dates from 1912.

transcript.speaker: Alison
transcript.text: The plants inside are lovely, but what is remarkable is the heating. There is no boiler anywhere on the site.

transcript.speaker: Alison
transcript.text: Warm water rises from a spring underneath the hill and is piped along the benches, exactly as the Edwardian gardeners arranged it.

transcript.speaker: Alison
transcript.text: Let me take you quickly round four areas, because each has something you need to know before you set off.

transcript.speaker: Alison
transcript.text: First, Fern Gully, the narrowest part of the old quarry, with steps cut into the rock and a stream beside them.

transcript.speaker: Alison
transcript.text: The ferns love it, but the stone turns dangerously slippery, so after heavy rain we simply close the gully and lock the top gate. Do check the board at the entrance.

transcript.speaker: Alison
transcript.text: Second, the Walled Herb Garden, which was the quarry manager's vegetable plot long before it grew lavender and thyme.

transcript.speaker: Alison
transcript.text: Every Thursday our chef cuts whatever he needs there for the cookery classes we run in the visitor centre, so please don't help yourselves on the way past.

transcript.speaker: Alison
transcript.text: Third, the Rock Terrace, where the alpine collection sits on the sunny side of the valley.

transcript.speaker: Alison
transcript.text: People tell me the terrace has the finest view, but it doesn't; the view belongs to the Lookout, further up. What the terrace has is exhausted soil, so from November the whole bed is being lifted and replanted.

transcript.speaker: Alison
transcript.text: And fourth, the Willow Maze, designed for us by pupils from the village primary school, and far harder than it looks.

transcript.speaker: Alison
transcript.text: Finally, a few practical points that will save you asking at the desk.

transcript.speaker: Alison
transcript.text: Free tours run twice a day. The old leaflet says they start at the shop; they don't any more. They now leave from the gatehouse, at eleven in the morning and at two.

transcript.speaker: Alison
transcript.text: There is a plant sale in the courtyard every Saturday. We used to hold it on Sunday, but Saturday proved far busier. Everything is grown by our volunteers.

transcript.speaker: Alison
transcript.text: And if you join as a member today you get evening access in summer: the public gates close at seven, but members may stay in the garden until 8.30.

transcript.speaker: Alison
transcript.text: That's enough from me. Maps are in the rack behind you, and I shall be at the gatehouse if you have questions. Do enjoy your morning.

sections.title: Tutorial: a research project on urban noise pollution
sections.context: Hai sinh viên Priya và Tom gặp giảng viên để báo cáo tiến độ dự án nghiên cứu về ô nhiễm tiếng ồn đô thị và bàn về báo cáo cuối kỳ.

transcript.speaker: Dr Nolan
transcript.text: Come in, both of you. So, the noise pollution project. Where have you got to since we last met?

transcript.speaker: Priya
transcript.text: Further than we expected, actually, although we had to change the whole design in the first week.

transcript.speaker: Dr Nolan
transcript.text: Oh? What went wrong?

transcript.speaker: Priya
transcript.text: We planned to run all three sites at once with the Class One sound level meters from the lab, but the acoustics module had booked both of them for a fortnight, so there was nothing available.

transcript.speaker: Dr Nolan
transcript.text: Ah. I did wonder whether the council would be the obstacle.

transcript.speaker: Tom
transcript.text: No, the council were helpful. They gave permission for all three locations in two days, and residents were keen to take part — nineteen questionnaires back out of twenty-five.

transcript.speaker: Priya
transcript.text: So the equipment was the only real problem. In the end we borrowed one meter from the engineering department and moved it from site to site.

transcript.speaker: Dr Nolan
transcript.text: Sensible. And your recording times — morning, afternoon and night, wasn't it?

transcript.speaker: Tom
transcript.text: Yes, and that's the second thing we changed. We started in late July and the readings looked wrong — the morning peak had almost disappeared.

transcript.speaker: Priya
transcript.text: It was the school holidays. The traffic was unusually light, and the whole picture was atypical, so we repeated everything in September once term had started.

transcript.speaker: Dr Nolan
transcript.text: Good. That's exactly the sort of judgement I want to see written up in the methodology, by the way. Don't hide it.

transcript.speaker: Tom
transcript.text: We wondered whether it made us look disorganised.

transcript.speaker: Dr Nolan
transcript.text: On the contrary. Now, the thing that concerns me slightly is the size of your sample. You have three sites, and how long at each?

transcript.speaker: Priya
transcript.text: Twenty minutes in each period, so an hour per site per day.

transcript.speaker: Dr Nolan
transcript.text: That's thin. I wouldn't add a fourth site — three is plenty, and a fourth would dilute your attention. And I certainly wouldn't repeat it in winter. What I would do is record for longer at each site: a continuous hour in each period rather than twenty minutes, and your averages become defensible.

transcript.speaker: Tom
transcript.text: That's manageable. We can do that over two weekends.

transcript.speaker: Dr Nolan
transcript.text: Then do. Now tell me what the data actually showed.

transcript.speaker: Priya
transcript.text: Shall I take the sites one by one? Market Street first. That's the pedestrianised shopping street with the delivery bay at the end.

transcript.speaker: Dr Nolan
transcript.text: I'd have expected it to be quiet, being pedestrianised.

transcript.speaker: Priya
transcript.text: So did we. On average it was moderate, but it produced the highest peak noise level of anywhere — a hundred and four decibels, when a refuse lorry reversed with its alarm going.

transcript.speaker: Dr Nolan
transcript.text: A single event, though.

transcript.speaker: Priya
transcript.text: Yes, and we say so. But it is the figure residents remember.

transcript.speaker: Dr Nolan
transcript.text: Fair. And Canal Bridge?

transcript.speaker: Tom
transcript.text: Canal Bridge was a disappointment. It's exposed, and the wind came straight down the water at the microphone; the foam shield wasn't enough and we lost three night recordings.

transcript.speaker: Priya
transcript.text: We've kept the figures in, but flagged them. It's easily our least reliable data, and I don't think we can draw much from it.

transcript.speaker: Dr Nolan
transcript.text: Be honest about that in the write-up and it costs you nothing. And the third — Riverside Estate, was it?

transcript.speaker: Tom
transcript.text: Riverside Estate, beside the ring road. Its daytime average wasn't the highest and its night average wasn't the lowest, but the gap between the two was enormous — twenty-six decibels between the afternoon and three in the morning.

transcript.speaker: Dr Nolan
transcript.text: Which is far bigger than either of the other sites.

transcript.speaker: Tom
transcript.text: By a long way. The ring road empties completely after midnight.

transcript.speaker: Dr Nolan
transcript.text: Now, you also ran a questionnaire. Did anything there surprise you?

transcript.speaker: Tom
transcript.text: One thing did. I'd assumed the older residents would complain most, as they're at home more. In fact they complained least, by a clear margin; the loudest complaints came from people in their twenties and thirties.

transcript.speaker: Priya
transcript.text: Tom thinks it's hearing loss. I think it's expectation — the younger residents are newer to the area and had imagined it would be quiet.

transcript.speaker: Dr Nolan
transcript.text: Both are plausible, and there's a literature on the second. Don't try to settle it with nineteen questionnaires, though. Report it and discuss it.

transcript.speaker: Tom
transcript.text: Understood.

transcript.speaker: Dr Nolan
transcript.text: Right, the presentation. How are you planning to show the results?

transcript.speaker: Priya
transcript.text: We discussed a bar chart per site, but it hides where the sites are in relation to each other, so instead we're colouring the readings onto a map of the city centre.

transcript.speaker: Dr Nolan
transcript.text: Much better. A map tells the story in one slide.

transcript.speaker: Dr Nolan
transcript.text: For the literature review, have you come across the Dutch work? There's a very good longitudinal study of noise complaints in Rotterdam — not Amsterdam, everybody cites the Amsterdam one — and it's the Rotterdam study that deals with exactly your age question.

transcript.speaker: Priya
transcript.text: Rotterdam. I'll find it this afternoon.

transcript.speaker: Dr Nolan
transcript.text: One last warning. Every year somebody hands me a two-page summary at the front. Your abstract must not be longer than 300 words, or I send it back unread.

transcript.speaker: Tom
transcript.text: Three hundred. Noted.

transcript.speaker: Dr Nolan
transcript.text: Good. Send me the revised methodology by the end of next week and we'll meet again once you've done the longer recordings.

sections.title: A short history of lighthouse engineering
sections.context: Bài giảng học thuật về lịch sử kỹ thuật xây dựng hải đăng, từ ngọn lửa cổ đại tới thời kỳ tự động hóa.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: Good afternoon. Today I want to trace the engineering of the lighthouse, because it is one of those rare structures where every improvement was paid for in lives.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: We begin with the Pharos, built on an island outside the harbour of Alexandria in the third century BC and standing, by most estimates, well over a hundred metres.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: At the very top the keepers kept an open fire burning all night. There is a persistent story that they burned oil, but the fuel available in that quantity was wood, brought across by boat and carried up an internal ramp.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: The light was thrown out to sea by a mirror. Ancient accounts describe it as polished bronze; later writers claimed glass, but glass of that size did not exist then.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: Move forward to medieval northern Europe and the fuel changes. Wood burns fast and unevenly, so the towers of Britain, the Netherlands and the Baltic burned coal instead, piled in an open iron basket called a chauffer.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: Coal is dense and burns hot, but the disadvantages were considerable.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: A single tower burned three or four hundred tonnes a year, hauled up the stairs by hand. And the greatest weakness of all of these fires was the smoke, which drifted across the flame and hid the light just when a ship close inshore most needed it.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: So the eighteenth century inherits a problem: how do you put a reliable light not on a headland but on a rock in open sea, where ships are actually lost?

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: The Eddystone reef, off southern England, is the classic case study: four towers were built there and each taught the next.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: The first, completed in 1698, was Henry Winstanley's: a highly decorated structure built of timber, bolted to the rock. He said he wished to be inside it during the greatest storm there ever was. In November 1703 he got his wish, and neither the tower nor Winstanley was seen again.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: The second, by John Rudyerd, was also largely timber but plainer and better shaped. It lasted almost fifty years, until the lantern caught fire in 1755.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: Two lessons were now clear: water destroys wood, and so does fire. The third tower would have to be stone.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: That tower, finished in 1759, was designed by John Smeaton, and it is the most important building in this story. He solved three problems at once.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: First, the shape. He wanted a natural form that resisted being pushed over, and he took the trunk of an oak, broad and curved at the base and tapering above. Every rock lighthouse since has that profile.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: Second, the fixing. Waves lift as well as push, so Smeaton cut each granite block so that it locked into its neighbours with dovetail joints, pinned with marble plugs. The tower behaves as one piece of rock rather than a pile of stones.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: Third, the mortar. Ordinary lime dissolves in the sea, so Smeaton experimented until he produced a lime containing a high proportion of clay, which would set hard under water. It is the direct ancestor of modern cement.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: It worked so well that when the rock beneath it began to fail in the eighteen-seventies, the Victorians rebuilt the upper part on shore, where you can still climb it.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: With the building problem solved, attention moved to the light, and the decisive figure is the French physicist Augustin Fresnel, in the eighteen-twenties.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: Until then lighthouses used metal reflectors behind an oil lamp, and most of the light was wasted. A conventional lens of the necessary size would have been impossibly heavy.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: Fresnel kept only the curved surface that does the work. His lens is a set of concentric rings of glass prisms, stepped like a beehive, which catch light escaping at wide angles and bend it into a single horizontal beam. It was up to four times brighter, and could be floated on mercury and turned by clockwork to give each station its own pattern of flashes.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: The lamp changed too. Vegetable oil gave way to mineral oil, and from the eighteen-seventies the brightest stations burned vaporised paraffin under pressure, which survived in remote places well into the twentieth century.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: Finally, electrification made a permanent human presence unnecessary, and from the nineteen-eighties the authorities automated station after station.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: In Britain, the final keepers came ashore from North Foreland in 1998, and every light in the country has been monitored remotely ever since.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: Next week we'll ask what satellite navigation has done to the argument for keeping these towers lit at all. Do read the Smeaton chapter first.

groups.intro:
EARLY LIGHTHOUSES

The Pharos of Alexandria (3rd century BC)
• The fire at the top of the tower burned ______ (31).
• The light was reflected out to sea by a mirror made of ______ (32).

Medieval towers in northern Europe
• The fire basket was filled with ______ (33).
• The main weakness of all open fires was the ______ (34), which hid the light.

The Eddystone reef
• The first tower, finished in 1698, was built of ______ (35) and was lost in a storm.

questions.prompt: The fire at the top of the Pharos burned ______.
questions.explanation: 'There is a persistent story that they burned oil, but the fuel almost certainly available in that quantity was wood' – dầu là thông tin sai bị bác bỏ.

questions.prompt: The light of the Pharos was reflected by a mirror made of ______.
questions.explanation: 'Ancient accounts describe it as polished bronze', còn giả thuyết gương thủy tinh bị loại vì thời đó chưa làm được.

questions.prompt: Medieval towers in northern Europe burned ______ in an open iron basket.
questions.explanation: 'The towers built along the coasts of Britain, the Netherlands and the Baltic burned coal instead, piled in an iron basket.'

questions.prompt: The greatest weakness of all these open fires was the ______.
questions.explanation: 'the greatest weakness of all of these fires... was the smoke, which drifted across the flame and hid the light.'

questions.prompt: The first Eddystone tower of 1698 was built of ______.
questions.explanation: 'it was a highly decorated structure built of timber, bolted to the rock', và bị bão cuốn đi năm 1703.

groups.instruction: Complete the sentences below. Write ONE WORD AND/OR A NUMBER for each answer.

questions.prompt: For the shape of his tower, Smeaton copied the trunk of an ______.
questions.explanation: 'he took the trunk of an oak, broad and curved at the base and tapering above it.'

questions.prompt: The granite blocks were locked into one another using ______ joints.
questions.explanation: 'Smeaton cut each granite block so that it locked into its neighbours with dovetail joints.'

questions.prompt: Smeaton created a lime mortar containing clay that would set hard under ______.
questions.explanation: 'he produced a lime containing a high proportion of clay, which would set hard under water.'

questions.prompt: Fresnel's lens was built from rings of glass ______ that bent the light into one beam.
questions.explanation: 'His lens is a set of concentric rings of glass prisms... which... bend it into a single horizontal beam.'

questions.prompt: The last lighthouse keepers in Britain came ashore in ______.
questions.explanation: 'In Britain, the final keepers came ashore from North Foreland in 1998.'
